tweets.text: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

New course: Build LLM applications that respond to user requests quickly by running on hardware designed for fast inference. This short course was built with @Cerebras and taught by @zhennydez , @duerr_seb , and @MilksandMatcha . When a model generates text, much of the time is spent moving its weights out of memory and into the compute units. Inference-optimized hardware minimizes that movement, making token generation several times faster than on a typical GPU setup. In this course, the hardware you'll use is Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, which is designed for fast inference by keeping the model's weights close to the compute units. Fast inference makes lengthy agentic workflows go faster, and also unlocks latency-sensitive, real-time applications like live translation and voice agents. Skills you'll gain: - Compare how GPUs, TPUs, and Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine each handle the memory-to-compute bottleneck - Build real-time applications powered by fast inference, including personalizing a webpage and running a multi-step workflow to analyze market signals - Adopt concrete habits for agentic coding with fast inference, keeping your sessions focused and steering the model more effectively My teams use Cerebras for several applications that are latency sensitive. “Loop engineering” is a hot buzzphrase after mentions of it by Boris Cherny (Claude Code’s creator) and Peter Steinberger (OpenClaw's creator) went viral on social media. Loops are now a key part of how we get AI agents to iterate at length to build software. In this letter, I’d like to share my 3 key loops, shown in the image below, for building 0-to-1 products. These loops guide not just how I build software, but also how I decide what software to build. Agentic coding loop: Given a product specification and optionally a set of evals (that is, a dataset against which to measure performance), we can have an AI agent write code, test its work, and keep iterating until the code is bug-free and meets its specification. This idea of closing the loop took off around the end of last year, and it has been a game changer in enabling coding agents to work longer productively without human intervention. For example, over the weekend, I was building an app for my daughter to practice typing, and my coding agent could easily work for around an hour, using a web browser to check what it had built multiple times before getting back to me, without needing my intervention. The engineering loop executes quickly. Every few minutes, the coding agent might build and test a new version of the software. I hear frequently from developers who are finding new ways to engineer more effective engineering loops. This is an active area of invention! Developer feedback loop: In this loop, a developer examines the current product and steers the coding agent to improve it. Last year, a lot of developers (including me) were acting as the QA (quality assurance) function for our coding agents, manually finding bugs and then asking the agent to fix them. But with coding agents much more able to test their own code, the amount of time we need to spend on this function has decreased significantly. This allows us to make higher-level product decisions, such as what key features to offer, where the UI needs improvement, and so on. The developer-feedback loop operates over time intervals between tens of minutes and hours — that's how frequently a developer might review a product and give feedback. In the case of the typing app, I changed my mind a few times about the visual design, what cat costumes she can unlock as she learns (she loves cats), and the user flow for a grown-up to log in and steer the child's learning experience. When a developer has a clear vision for what to build, it is still a lot of work to translate that vision into a specification for a coding agent to implement. Further, after the developer has seen an implementation, they might update (or perhaps clarify) the spec to steer it toward what they want. If you find that the system repeatedly runs into certain problems, building a set of evals for the agent becomes useful. AI-native teams are increasingly using AI to help shape product direction, for example, automating the gathering and analysis of usage data, summarizing written and verbal customer feedback, or carrying out competitive analysis. However, for pretty much all the products I’m involved in, I see humans as having a significant context advantage over current AI systems — we know a lot more than the AI system about the users and the context the product has to operate in — and thus humans play a critical role. Many people describe this human contribution as “taste,” but I prefer to think of it as humans having a context advantage, since that gives us a clearer path to helping AI systems get better. This also speaks to why this step can’t be automated: So long as the human knows something the AI does not, human-in-the-loop is needed to to inject that knowledge into the system. External feedback loop: This includes a wide range of tactics like asking a few friends for feedback, launching to alpha testers, or putting the code into production with A/B testing. These tactics are usually slow, rarely taking less than hours and sometimes taking days or even weeks. This data informs the developer vision, which in turn continues to drive the detailed product spec, which in turn drives the coding agent. With coding agents speeding up software development, more engineers are starting to play a partial product management role. For many engineers who are growing into this role, the hardest part is shaping the product vision and striking a balance between building (bridging the gap between vision and spec) and getting user feedback to evolve the vision. It is important to do both! I will write more about how to do this in future posts, but for now, I find it encouraging that engineers are playing an expanded role (just as product managers and designers now do more engineering). Over the last two weeks, both the U.S. Government and Anthropic took significant actions that demonstrated their power to control access to AI by restricting what others can do with frontier models. This has been one of those moments that, once seen, will be hard to unsee, and it is significantly accelerating many businesses’ and nation states’ efforts to ensure reliable access to AI that no one else can terminate. Anthropic first released Claude Fable 5, a version of its Mythos model with additional guardrails, including some restrictions that seem well justified on safety grounds (such as limitations on applying it to hacking, bioweapons, and so forth). However, it also restricted developers’ ability to use it to build competing LLM technology. This move was concerning, given that the whole AI community, including Anthropic, has benefitted tremendously from open research — indeed, the AI revolution was kicked off by my former team (Google Brain) freely publishing the Transformers paper! Imagine if Microsoft’s terms of use barred anyone from using their tools to build competitive software, or if Google barred using it to search for information to work on competing search engines. Anthropic’s argument that it was unsafe for others to be able to make advances in AI also rang hollow. Initially, Anthropic silently degraded Fable 5’s performance for users detected to be working on LLM research through invisible interventions that weakened the model’s outputs without notifying the user. After significant backlash, it walked back this decision and decided to be transparent when it did this, but it still refuses to use its latest capabilities to help AI researchers. This move represents a raw demonstration of power by Anthropic. It has used “safety” arguments to hinder potential competitors. Platforms succeed when they are viewed as stable, reliable partners that one can build on. The sudden rule changes by Anthropic (including a mandatory 30 day data retention policy for Fable usage) have made developers wonder about the stability of building on any one proprietary LLM provider, not just Anthropic. The U.S. Government then shortly followed with an even greater demonstration of power. It used the Commerce Department’s authority to regulate technologies that may be national security threats to restrict exports of Mythos and Fable, requiring a license for use by any foreign national, whether inside or outside of the U.S., including employees of Anthropic. This led Anthropic to disable access to Fable to all users worldwide. Sam Altman pointed out, referring to Anthropic, “It is clearly incredible marketing to say, ‘We have built a bomb, we are about to drop it on your head. We will sell you a bomb shelter for $100 million.’” But when one engages in this type of fear-based marketing, it increases the odds that the U.S. Government will agree with you and slap export controls on the bomb you say you have built. To be clear, I don't think Anthropic has built anything like a bomb, and I don't think export controls on Fable are appropriate. However, following the U.S. Government making this move, many nations, including U.S. allies, saw how the U.S. can suddenly yank their access to AI models. In many capitals around the world, this has spurred discussions on AI sovereignty and how others can ensure uninterrupted access to this critical technology. For decades, many nations were comfortable having many parts of their supply chain rely on the U.S., China, and other major producers. Once a nation issues a threat, or takes action, to limit other nations’ access, other nations will rationally try to secure alternatives. For decades, semiconductor manufacturing in China made slow progress; once the U.S. moved to limit China’s access, China’s efforts kicked into high gear. Similarly, once China threatened U.S. access to rare earth minerals, U.S. efforts to secure alternatives accelerated. Now that it has become crystal clear that private U.S. companies and the U.S. government can limit, in short order, other nations’ access to frontier AI models, the incentive of others to invest more in alternatives like open source grows significantly. Of course, training frontier models is not easy, so it remains to be seen how successful they are, but we have crossed the rubicon. Satya Nadella wrote an essay about the importance of building a healthy ecosystem on top of frontier AI technology. I heartily agree with him, and hope this week’s events will ultimately prove to be constructive steps toward this. I hope we can build a more free, more open world, where research is freely shared, and laws and societal norms shape a level playing field that allows everyone to make progress. A silver lining of the events of these past two weeks is now that everyone better realizes key points of instability of the current system, we can all work to create a more stable foundation. The IMO is today and 5.6 one-shotting a perfect score isn't even news. Where will we be next year? Edgar Dobriban (@EdgarDobriban) AI has helped resolve an important question in statistics. In the area of multiple hypothesis testing, the goal of controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) has been introduced in a seminal paper by Benjamini and Hochberg (1995). They also introduced a method (the Benjamini-Hochberg or BH method) and proved it controls the FDR. This method has been widely adopted in modern high-throughput science, including in genomics, astronomy, economics, etc. The paper has has garnered more than 130,000 citations to date. However Benjamini and Hochberg showed FDR control only when the data for the individual tests are *independent*. In practice, these data are often dependent; a good example is data on genetic variants due to linkage disequilibrium. Later work has focused on extending the validity of the BH procedure, e.g., to a form of positive dependence by Benjamini and Yekutieli (2001). The question of when the BH procedure controls the FDR has remained open. Over the last twenty years, many authors, including Reiner-Benaim (2007), Kim and van de Wiel (2008), Benjamini (2010), Sarkar (2023), Sarkar and Zhang (2025), have conjectured that the BH procedure controls the FDR for two-sided tests using any correlated Gaussian data. These authors have presented both theoretical and empirical evidence supporting, but not directly showing, the conjecture. With the help of AI (specifically GPT-5.6 Sol Pro), I have settled the question in the negative: The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure does *not* generally control the false discovery rate at the desired level for correlated two-sided Gaussian tests. This was done by exhibiting a Gaussian factor model for which, at a nominal level alpha=0.01, the false discovery rate is proved to be FDR>0.0104. There is a lot of interesting commentary to be made: 1. This result should be of interest to everybody in the field of statistics. Emmanuel Candes of Stanford University once called the false discovery rate and the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure "one of the two most important developments in statistics after 1950" (the other being James-Stein shrinkage). The present conjecture is probably the most central question about FDR/BH that was unresolved to date. 2. GPT-5.6 one-shot the problem after 90 minutes of reasoning, whereas with 5.5 I was not able to solve it even after iterating with multiple parallel agents for perhaps 20 hours. So the capability improvement is quite real. Exciting times to live in! 3. The argument is not especially surprising, but it does combine an asymptotic approach (standard for FDR analysis, see e.g., Genovese and Wasserman, Efron, etc) with a numerical certificate in a way that would be pretty non-standard in the field. Once we have the specific example, then straightforward simulations also support that the false discovery rate is indeed higher than the nominal value (see attached fig). 4. The current degree of violation over the nominal level is relatively small (0.104 vs 0.1). So the importance of this result is mainly conceptual. The practical implications remain to be determined. Overall, an exciting development! Preprint is available here ( faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp… ) and will be on arxiv tonight; supporting code is here ( github.com/dobriban/BH ). — https://nitter.net/EdgarDobriban/status/2077082912021786660#m

Here's the closing message I sent to everyone today. My dear friends! Today’s my last day at OpenAI. I have been thinking a lot about what I wanted to say in my final remarks to the company. Here are a few things I hope everyone takes deeply to heart. 1. For All of Humanity. What we have been building here is an opportunity to improve the human condition unlike any other in history. It’s easy to get distracted by the wealth and power that comes with this. It’s easy to focus on the already wealthy and powerful in the world, because they demand so much of our attention as customers or lawmakers or competitors. Nonetheless, do not lose sight of the “all” in “all of humanity.” Our mission for everyone. Working people. People in poverty. People who dream of a better life. What we are building can help them. It is our mission to ensure that it does. To that end, yesterday I donated a major gift to GiveDirectly, a charity that makes direct cash transfers to people in poverty in Africa and in the United States. This is a highly effective way of helping people; I encourage others to consider giving as well. 2. Risk Is Our Business. Technology changes the security equilibrium of the world profoundly and creates new risks. Some of these risks will directly result from AI; many others will result from other fields of science and engineering that are accelerated by AI. Risk is inextricable from progress. It is not a reason to turn our back on progress. I think, from time to time, of a speech from Captain Kirk in the original Star Trek—“Risk is our business,” he says about humanity as a whole. I believe this is true. But we should also be cognizant of the risks and we should actively manage them. We can simultaneously believe that it will require extraordinary effort to accomplish the safety and security of humanity, while committing to making that effort in support of our work to advance the technological frontier. The question of progress and safety is not either/or. It is definitively “both.” 3. The Consent of the Governed. OpenAI, and especially the OpenAI Foundation, will be among the most important organizations in the world. The level of power concentrated here will be like the power of a state. It demands a level of accountability that exceeds that of an ordinary company. I encourage OpenAI to pursue a path of governance innovation that makes it progressively more democratic and more beholden to the consent of the governed. All of humanity will be impacted by the work here; all of humanity should have some way to weigh in eventually. There is no roadmap for what form this should take. This is an ideal. But I hold it entirely. Thank you all again so much for being a part of an unbelievable nine year journey with me. To Safe AGI!

For over two years, the largest open code dataset was The Stack v2… until today. 🥞 The Stack v3 is out: the largest open code dataset ever released: 114 TB, 770 languages, 224M repositories, ~5T tokens of deduplicated and filtered source code. Fully open, no restrictively licensed code included. The upgrade: - v2 (2024): 68 TB raw -> 2 TB / ~550B tokens, 618 languages filtered - v3 (2026): 114 TB raw -> 15.9 TB / ~5T tokens, 713 languages filtered C++ x15, TypeScript x7.5, Rust x7, Python x4.8. Even the COBOL corner of GitHub got a bigger slice. Part of that is two fresh years of open source. Part of it is a bug we found in v2's deduplication - story below. 👀 Things that make v3 different: 1. Contents inline. The #1 complaint about v2 was "cool dataset, where's the actual code?" v2 shipped file IDs from the Software Heritage graph, and fetching contents was a DIY treasure hunt. v3 is self-contained: sources embedded directly, one row = one repository. Download finishes -> you start training. 2. Fresh crawl. v2 was a 2023 snapshot of even older crawls. v3 is a direct re-crawl of GitHub at the latest commit, completed by August 2025: 224M repositories, 44B files. Forks were only included if they had 5+ stars. Two ways in: 🥞 stack-v3-train - near-deduplicated, quality-filtered, PII-redacted, contents inline. Point load_dataset at it and go. huggingface.co/datasets/Hugg… 🏗 stack-v3-full - the entire 114 TB corpus as an HF Storage Bucket: every duplicate kept with cluster IDs, stubs for excluded files. Roll your own dedup, filters, and mixes. huggingface.co/buckets/Huggi… The record isn't really ours to claim - it's millions of everyone's repositories, neatly stacked. Thanks to every developer who keeps their code public, the BigCode community, and friends who built the infrastructure that made this possible!

@MIT_CSAIL 's @a1zhang and @lateinteraction trained a model to generalize 8-32x past its training length. The research credits the harness, the scaffolding around the model, not the model itself. Train it only on short tasks, and it still handles far longer ones. That works because the harness keeps every model call close to what it was trained on. It offloads the bulk context into a code environment and keeps the results of its smaller sub-tasks out of the main chat, so the model never drowns in its own history. A few things that held up: > trains short, runs 8-32x longer > transfers across different domains > training costs 1.5-3x more Context rot, the decay your agent hits as history piles up, is often this scaffolding problem, not a weak model. So, > How do you tell rot from a model that is simply too weak? > When does adding a harness backfire? > What is the one check to run before you pay for a bigger model? highlights.text_fr: Une méthode utile pour travailler avec les grands modèles de langage est la session de "longue divagation". Parfois, le modèle a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez de faire, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime me pencher en arrière, passer en mode vocal et simplement divaguer pendant environ 10 minutes, un vrai fouillis, tout est permis, flux de conscience total. Parfois, je le déclare au début, quelque chose comme "passage à la reconnaissance vocale, désolé pour les fautes de frappe...". Parfois, j'en fais une petite interview en quelques tours. Mais je trouve que les grands modèles de langage sont étonnamment doués pour reconstituer de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de vos propres pensées embrouillées sort un peu plus clair que ce que vous aviez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la connexion esprit-machine et que vous avez moins à corriger par la suite.
highlights.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.
highlights.decryptage: Pour mieux se faire comprendre des IA, il est parfois utile de parler longuement, même de manière désordonnée, car l'IA peut mieux en tirer l'essentiel.
highlights.highlight_reason: Astuce très pratique d'un expert pour améliorer l'interaction avec les IA génératives, applicable par tous les débutants.

tips.text_fr: L'"ingénierie en boucle" ("Loop engineering") est un mot à la mode après que les mentions de Boris Cherny (créateur de Claude Code) et Peter Steinberger (créateur d'OpenClaw) soient devenues virales sur les réseaux sociaux. Les boucles sont maintenant une partie essentielle de la façon dont nous faisons en sorte que les agents IA itèrent longuement pour construire des logiciels. Dans cette lettre, je tiens à partager mes 3 boucles clés, montrées dans l'image ci-dessous, pour construire des produits "0 à 1". Ces boucles guident non seulement la façon dont je construis des logiciels, mais aussi comment je décide quels logiciels construire. Boucle de codage agentique : Étant donné une spécification de produit et éventuellement un ensemble d'évaluations (c'est-à-dire un jeu de données contre lequel mesurer les performances), nous pouvons demander à un agent IA d'écrire du code, de tester son travail et de continuer à itérer jusqu'à ce que le code soit sans bug et conforme à sa spécification. Cette idée de "fermer la boucle" a pris son essor vers la fin de l'année dernière, et cela a révolutionné la façon dont les agents de codage peuvent travailler plus longtemps de manière productive sans intervention humaine. Par exemple, ce week-end, je construisais une application pour ma fille pour pratiquer la dactylographie, et mon agent de codage a pu facilement travailler pendant environ une heure, en utilisant un navigateur web pour vérifier ce qu'il avait construit plusieurs fois avant de me revenir, sans avoir besoin de mon intervention. L'ingénierie en boucle s'exécute rapidement. Toutes les quelques minutes, l'agent de codage peut construire et tester une nouvelle version du logiciel. J'entends fréquemment parler de développeurs qui trouvent de nouvelles façons d'ingénier des boucles d'ingénierie plus efficaces. C'est un domaine d'invention actif ! Boucle de retour d'information du développeur : Dans cette boucle, un développeur examine le produit actuel et dirige l'agent de codage pour l'améliorer. L'année dernière, beaucoup de développeurs (y compris moi) agissaient en tant que fonction QA (assurance qualité) pour nos agents de codage, trouvant manuellement des bugs puis demandant à l'agent de les corriger. Mais avec les agents de codage beaucoup plus capables de tester leur propre code, le temps que nous devons consacrer à cette fonction a considérablement diminué. Cela nous permet de prendre des décisions produit de plus haut niveau, telles que quelles fonctionnalités clés offrir, où l'interface utilisateur nécessite une amélioration, etc. La boucle de retour d'information du développeur fonctionne sur des intervalles de temps entre dix minutes et plusieurs heures – c'est la fréquence à laquelle un développeur peut examiner un produit et donner son avis. Dans le cas de l'application de dactylographie, j'ai changé d'avis plusieurs fois sur le design visuel, les costumes de chat qu'elle peut débloquer en apprenant (elle adore les chats), et le flux utilisateur pour qu'un adulte se connecte et dirige l'expérience d'apprentissage de l'enfant. Lorsqu'un développeur a une vision claire de ce qu'il faut construire, il faut encore beaucoup de travail pour traduire cette vision en une spécification qu'un agent de codage puisse implémenter. De plus, après que le développeur a vu une implémentation, il pourrait mettre à jour (ou peut-être clarifier) la spécification pour l'orienter vers ce qu'il veut. Si vous constatez que le système rencontre à plusieurs reprises certains problèmes, la création d'un ensemble d'évaluations pour l'agent devient utile. Les équipes natives de l'IA utilisent de plus en plus l'IA pour aider à façonner la direction du produit, par exemple, en automatisant la collecte et l'analyse des données d'utilisation, en résumant les commentaires clients écrits et verbaux, ou en effectuant des analyses concurrentielles. Cependant, pour à peu près tous les produits auxquels je suis impliqué, je vois les humains comme ayant un avantage contextuel significatif par rapport aux systèmes d'IA actuels – nous en savons beaucoup plus que le système d'IA sur les utilisateurs et le contexte dans lequel le produit doit fonctionner – et donc les humains jouent un rôle critique. Beaucoup de gens décrivent cette contribution humaine comme du "goût", mais je préfère penser qu'il s'agit d'humains ayant un avantage contextuel, car cela nous donne une voie plus claire pour aider les systèmes d'IA à s'améliorer. Cela parle aussi de pourquoi cette étape ne peut pas être automatisée : Tant que l'humain sait quelque chose que l'IA ne sait pas, l'humain dans la boucle est nécessaire pour injecter cette connaissance dans le système. Boucle de retour d'information externe : Cela comprend un large éventail de tactiques comme demander des commentaires à quelques amis, lancer des tests alpha, ou mettre le code en production avec des tests A/B. Ces tactiques sont généralement lentes, prenant rarement moins de quelques heures et parfois des jours voire des semaines. Ces données éclairent la vision du développeur, qui à son tour continue de piloter la spécification détaillée du produit, qui à son tour pilote l'agent de codage. Avec les agents de codage qui accélèrent le développement logiciel, de plus en plus d'ingénieurs commencent à jouer un rôle partiel de gestion de produit. Pour de nombreux ingénieurs qui évoluent dans ce rôle, la partie la plus difficile est de façonner la vision du produit et de trouver un équilibre entre la construction (combler le fossé entre la vision et la spécification) et l'obtention des commentaires des utilisateurs pour faire évoluer la vision. Il est important de faire les deux ! J'écrirai davantage sur la façon de faire cela dans de futurs posts, mais pour l'instant, je trouve encourageant que les ingénieurs jouent un rôle élargi (tout comme les chefs de produit et les designers font maintenant plus d'ingénierie). [Texte original : The Batch]
tips.text_original: “Loop engineering” is a hot buzzphrase after mentions of it by Boris Cherny (Claude Code’s creator) and Peter Steinberger (OpenClaw's creator) went viral on social media. Loops are now a key part of how we get AI agents to iterate at length to build software. In this letter, I’d like to share my 3 key loops, shown in the image below, for building 0-to-1 products. These loops guide not just how I build software, but also how I decide what software to build. Agentic coding loop: Given a product specification and optionally a set of evals (that is, a dataset against which to measure performance), we can have an AI agent write code, test its work, and keep iterating until the code is bug-free and meets its specification. This idea of closing the loop took off around the end of last year, and it has been a game changer in enabling coding agents to work longer productively without human intervention. For example, over the weekend, I was building an app for my daughter to practice typing, and my coding agent could easily work for around an hour, using a web browser to check what it had built multiple times before getting back to me, without needing my intervention. The engineering loop executes quickly. Every few minutes, the coding agent might build and test a new version of the software. I hear frequently from developers who are finding new ways to engineer more effective engineering loops. This is an active area of invention! Developer feedback loop: In this loop, a developer examines the current product and steers the coding agent to improve it. Last year, a lot of developers (including me) were acting as the QA (quality assurance) function for our coding agents, manually finding bugs and then asking the agent to fix them. But with coding agents much more able to test their own code, the amount of time we need to spend on this function has decreased significantly. This allows us to make higher-level product decisions, such as what key features to offer, where the UI needs improvement, and so on. The developer-feedback loop operates over time intervals between tens of minutes and hours — that's how frequently a developer might review a product and give feedback. In the case of the typing app, I changed my mind a few times about the visual design, what cat costumes she can unlock as she learns (she loves cats), and the user flow for a grown-up to log in and steer the child's learning experience. When a developer has a clear vision for what to build, it is still a lot of work to translate that vision into a specification for a coding agent to implement. Further, after the developer has seen an implementation, they might update (or perhaps clarify) the spec to steer it toward what they want. If you find that the system repeatedly runs into certain problems, building a set of evals for the agent becomes useful. AI-native teams are increasingly using AI to help shape product direction, for example, automating the gathering and analysis of usage data, summarizing written and verbal customer feedback, or carrying out competitive analysis. However, for pretty much all the products I’m involved in, I see humans as having a significant context advantage over current AI systems — we know a lot more than the AI system about the users and the context the product has to operate in — and thus humans play a critical role. Many people describe this human contribution as “taste,” but I prefer to think of it as humans having a context advantage, since that gives us a clearer path to helping AI systems get better. This also speaks to why this step can’t be automated: So long as the human knows something the AI does not, human-in-the-loop isHeeded to inject that knowledge into the system. External feedback loop: This includes a wide range of tactics like asking a few friends for feedback, launching to alpha testers, or putting the code into production with A/B testing. These tactics are usually slow, rarely taking less than hours and sometimes taking days or even weeks. This data informs the developer vision, which in turn continues to drive the detailed product spec, which in turn drives the coding agent. With coding agents speeding up software development, more engineers are starting to play a partial product management role. For many engineers who are growing into this role, the hardest part is shaping the product vision and striking a balance between building (bridging the gap between vision and spec) and getting user feedback to evolve the vision. It is important to do both! I will write more about how to do this in future posts, but for now, I find it encouraging that engineers are playing an expanded role (just as product managers and designers now do more engineering). [Original text: The Batch]

idees.text_fr: Adam Thierer avait écrit le livre de référence sur "l'innovation sans permission". Nous obtenons les meilleures idées quand nous n'avons pas à demander la permission du gouvernement à l'avance pour inventer. Protéger l'IA open source est maintenant un élément essentiel pour assurer cela. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) Nous sommes à un carrefour critique dans le débat sur la gouvernance de l'IA aux États-Unis, et il semble que nous nous rapprochions d'une bataille très sérieuse pour savoir si les modèles open source seront même autorisés dans un environnement où un nouveau régime de licence de facto a pris forme. En l'absence de cadres législatifs formels du Congrès ou de règles claires de l'administration (comme la révision de la règle de diffusion), il semble que nous soyons laissés avec un processus d'examen des modèles sporadique, arbitraire et non transparent. La fiction des accords "volontaires" plane sur ce débat, et certains grands développeurs de modèles montrent déjà une volonté incroyable de faire des courbettes pour satisfaire les responsables / ordres liés à la sécurité nationale dont le reste d'entre nous n'a pas connaissance. C'est un processus très opaque. Et ces développeurs de modèles sont censés jouer le jeu avec ces responsables, sinon leurs modèles seront retirés du marché ou retardés pendant de longues périodes. Ou ils perdront tous les contrats d'approvisionnement gouvernementaux qu'ils ont. Il n'y a rien de "volontaire" à cela quand cette épée de Damoclès plane dans la pièce. Alors que ce désordre s'aggrave, à un moment donné, la question de savoir comment gérer les modèles open source deviendra plus claire car elle devra l'être. J'ai même entendu des rumeurs récemment selon lesquelles quelque chose pourrait venir de l'administration à ce sujet pour y remédier. Il va sans dire que si ce nouveau régime informel d'examen des modèles d'IA s'étend et prend davantage de caractéristiques / exigences de pré-vérification, il est difficile de voir comment les acteurs "open source" pourraient se conformer à une telle licence quasi-IA. Plus précisément, si ce nouveau régime ambigu est accompagné d'une présomption générale de "restreindre jusqu'à autorisation", alors ce serait la fin pour l'open source. C'est un chemin très sombre pour notre pays. Pire encore, bien sûr, serait une mesure des responsables de la sécurité nationale pour restreindre plus directement les modèles et capacités "open source". Si cela se produit, alors nous serions de retour au cœur d'une bataille de type "Clipper Chip", le long des lignes de ce que nous avons vu à la fin des années 1990. C'est un chemin beaucoup plus sombre pour l'Amérique. Pendant ce temps, les développeurs "open source" n'ont pas d'"actions dorées" ni d'autres sucreries à offrir au gouvernement pour faire disparaître leurs problèmes. Soyons clairs : si notre gouvernement prend le chemin sombre, ce sera la bataille la plus importante pour la liberté computationnelle de l'époque moderne. Il est temps que les gens prennent position pour défendre l'open source avant qu'il ne soit trop tard. — https://nitter.net/AdamThierer/status/2075237102099251371#m

Lacking formal congressional statutory frameworks or clear administration rules (like the diffusion rule revision), we appear to be left with a sporadic, arbitrary, non-transparent process for model review. The fiction of “voluntary” agreements hangs over this debate, and some large model developers are already showing an incredible willingness to bend over backwards to accommodate national security-related officials / orders that the rest of us are not privy to. Or they will lose any government procurement contracts they have. There is nothing “voluntary” about it when that Sword of Damocles hangs in the room. As this mess worsens, at some point the question of how to handle open source models will come into sharper focus because it will have to. I've even heard some rumors lately that something may be coming from the admin on this front to address this. Needless to say, if this informal new AI model review regime expands and takes on more pre-vetting characteristics / requirements, it is hard to see how open source players could comply with such quasi-licensing of AI models. Specifically, if this ambiguous new regime is accompanied by a general presumption of ‘restrict-until-permitted,’ then that would spell doom for open source. That is a very dark path for our country. Worse yet, of course, would be a move by national security officials to more directly restrict open source models and capabilities. Meanwhile, open source developers have no “golden shares” or other goodies to offer the government to make their problems go away. Let’s be clear: If our government takes the dark path, it will become the single most important battle over computational freedom of modern times. idees.text_fr: Au cours des deux dernières semaines, le gouvernement américain et Anthropic ont tous deux pris des mesures importantes qui ont démontré leur pouvoir de contrôler l'accès à l'IA en restreignant ce que d'autres peuvent faire avec les modèles de pointe. Ce fut l'un de ces moments qui, une fois vus, seront difficiles à oublier, et cela accélère considérablement les efforts de nombreuses entreprises et nations pour garantir un accès fiable à l'IA que personne d'autre ne peut interrompre. Anthropic a d'abord publié Claude Fable 5, une version de son modèle Mythos avec des garde-fous supplémentaires, y compris certaines restrictions qui semblent bien justifiées pour des raisons de sécurité (comme les limitations sur son application au piratage, aux armes biologiques, etc.). Cependant, cela a également restreint la capacité des développeurs à l'utiliser pour créer une technologie LLM concurrente. Cette décision était préoccupante, étant donné que toute la communauté de l'IA, y compris Anthropic, a énormément bénéficié de la recherche ouverte – en effet, la révolution de l'IA a été lancée par mon ancienne équipe (Google Brain) en publiant librement le papier Transformers ! Imaginez si les conditions d'utilisation de Microsoft interdisaient à quiconque d'utiliser leurs outils pour créer des logiciels concurrents, ou si Google interdisait de les utiliser pour rechercher des informations afin de travailler sur des moteurs de recherche concurrents. L'argument d'Anthropic selon lequel il était dangereux pour d'autres de pouvoir faire des progrès en IA a également sonné creux. Initialement, Anthropic a silencieusement dégradé les performances de Fable 5 pour les utilisateurs détectés comme travaillant sur la recherche LLM par des interventions invisibles qui ont affaibli les sorties du modèle sans en informer l'utilisateur. Après une réaction négative importante, elle est revenue sur cette décision et a décidé d'être transparente lorsqu'elle le faisait, mais refuse toujours d'utiliser ses dernières capacités pour aider les chercheurs en IA. Ce mouvement représente une démonstration brute de pouvoir par Anthropic. Elle a utilisé des arguments de "sécurité" pour entraver des concurrents potentiels. Les plateformes réussissent lorsqu'elles sont considérées comme des partenaires stables et fiables sur lesquels on peut construire. Les changements soudains de règles par Anthropic (y compris une politique obligatoire de conservation des données de 30 jours pour l'utilisation de Fable) ont amené les développeurs à s'interroger sur la stabilité de la construction sur un fournisseur de LLM propriétaire, pas seulement Anthropic. Le gouvernement américain a ensuite suivi avec une démonstration de pouvoir encore plus grande. Il a utilisé l'autorité du Département du Commerce pour réglementer les technologies susceptibles de constituer des menaces pour la sécurité nationale afin de restreindre les exportations de Mythos et Fable, exigeant une licence pour leur utilisation par tout ressortissant étranger, qu'il soit à l'intérieur ou à l'extérieur des États-Unis, y compris les employés d'Anthropic. Cela a conduit Anthropic à désactiver l'accès à Fable pour tous les utilisateurs dans le monde. Sam Altman a souligné, en parlant d'Anthropic : "C'est clairement un marketing incroyable de dire : 'Nous avons construit une bombe, nous sommes sur le point de vous la lancer. Nous vous vendrons un abri anti-bombes pour 100 millions de dollars.'" Mais lorsque l'on s'engage dans ce type de marketing basé sur la peur, cela augmente les chances que le gouvernement américain soit d'accord avec vous et impose des contrôles à l'exportation sur la bombe que vous dites avoir construite. Pour être clair, je ne pense pas qu'Anthropic ait construit quoi que ce soit qui ressemble à une bombe, et je ne pense pas que les contrôles à l'exportation sur Fable soient appropriés. Cependant, suite à cette décision du gouvernement américain, de nombreuses nations, y compris des alliés des États-Unis, ont vu comment les États-Unis peuvent soudainement leur couper l'accès aux modèles d'IA. Dans de nombreuses capitales du monde, cela a suscité des discussions sur la souveraineté de l'IA et sur la manière dont les autres peuvent garantir un accès ininterrompu à cette technologie critique. Pendant des décennies, de nombreuses nations se sont contentées d'avoir de nombreuses parties de leur chaîne d'approvisionnement dépendantes des États-Unis, de la Chine et d'autres grands producteurs. Une fois qu'une nation menace ou agit pour limiter l'accès des autres nations, celles-ci chercheront rationnellement des alternatives. Pendant des décennies, la fabrication de semi-conducteurs en Chine a progressé lentement ; une fois que les États-Unis ont agi pour limiter l'accès de la Chine, les efforts de la Chine se sont intensifiés. idees.text_original: Over the last two weeks, both the U.S. Government and Anthropic took significant actions that demonstrated their power to control access to AI by restricting what others can do with frontier models. This has been one of those moments that, once seen, will be hard to unsee, and it is significantly accelerating many businesses’ and nation states’ efforts to ensure reliable access to AI that no one else can terminate. Anthropic first released Claude Fable 5, a version of its Mythos model with additional guardrails, including some restrictions that seem well justified on safety grounds (such as limitations on applying it to hacking, bioweapons, and so forth). However, it also restricted developers’ ability to use it to build competing LLM technology. This move was concerning, given that the whole AI community, including Anthropic, has benefitted tremendously from open research — indeed, the AI revolution was kicked off by my former team (Google Brain) freely publishing the Transformers paper! Imagine if Microsoft’s terms of use barred anyone from using their tools to build competitive software, or if Google barred using it to search for information to work on competing search engines. Anthropic’s argument that it was unsafe for others to be able to make advances in AI also rang hollow. Initially, Anthropic silently degraded Fable 5’s performance for users detected to be working on LLM research through invisible interventions that weakened the model’s outputs without notifying the user. After significant backlash, it walked back this decision and decided to be transparent when it did this, but it still refuses to use its latest capabilities to help AI researchers. This move represents a raw demonstration of power by Anthropic. It has used “safety” arguments to hinder potential competitors. Platforms succeed when they are viewed as stable, reliable partners that one can build on. The sudden rule changes by Anthropic (including a mandatory 30 day data retention policy for Fable usage) have made developers wonder about the stability of building on any one proprietary LLM provider, not just Anthropic. The U.S. Government then shortly followed with an even greater demonstration of power. It used the Commerce Department’s authority to regulate technologies that may be national security threats to restrict exports of Mythos and Fable, requiring a license for use by any foreign national, whether inside or outside of the U.S., including employees of Anthropic. This led Anthropic to disable access to Fable to all users worldwide. Sam Altman pointed out, referring to Anthropic, “It is clearly incredible marketing to say, ‘We have built a bomb, we are about to drop it on your head. We will sell you a bomb shelter for $100 million.’” But when one engages in this type of fear-based marketing, it increases the odds that the U.S. Government will agree with you and slap export controls on the bomb you say you have built. To be clear, I don't think Anthropic has built anything like a bomb, and I don't think export controls on Fable are appropriate. However, following the U.S. Government making this move, many nations, including U.S. allies, saw how the U.S. can suddenly yank their access to AI models. In many capitals around the world, this has spurred discussions on AI sovereignty and how others can ensure uninterrupted access to this critical technology. For decades, many nations were comfortable having many parts of their supply chain rely on the U.S., China, and other major producers. Once a nation issues a threat, or takes action, to limit other nations’ access to frontier AI models, the incentive of others to invest more in alternatives like open source grows significantly. Of course, training frontier models is not easy, so it remains to be seen how successful they are, but we have crossed the rubicon. Satya Nadella wrote an essay about the importance of building a healthy ecosystem on top of frontier AI technology. I heartily agree with him, and hope this week’s events will ultimately prove to be constructive steps toward this. I hope we can build a more free, more open world, where research is freely shared, and laws and societal norms shape a level playing field that allows everyone to make progress. A silver lining of the events of these past two weeks is now that everyone better realizes key points of instability of the current system, we can all work to create a more stable foundation. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]

Edgar Dobriban (@EdgarDobriban) L'IA a aidé à résoudre une question importante en statistiques. Dans le domaine des tests d'hypothèses multiples, l'objectif de contrôler le taux de fausse découverte (FDR) a été introduit dans un article séminal par Benjamini et Hochberg (1995). Ils ont également introduit une méthode (la méthode Benjamini-Hochberg ou BH) et ont prouvé qu'elle contrôle le FDR. Cette méthode a été largement adoptée dans la science moderne à haut débit, y compris en génomique, astronomie, économie, etc. L'article a recueilli plus de 130 000 citations à ce jour. Cependant, Benjamini et Hochberg n'ont montré le contrôle du FDR que lorsque les données pour les tests individuels sont *indépendantes*. En pratique, ces données sont souvent dépendantes ; un bon exemple est les données sur les variants génétiques dues à la déséquilibre de liaison. Les travaux ultérieurs se sont concentrés sur l'extension de la validité de la procédure BH, par exemple, à une forme de dépendance positive par Benjamini et Yekutieli (2001). La question de savoir quand la procédure BH contrôle le FDR est restée ouverte. Au cours des vingt dernières années, de nombreux auteurs, dont Reiner-Benaim (2007), Kim et van de Wiel (2008), Benjamini (2010), Sarkar (2023), Sarkar et Zhang (2025), ont émis l'hypothèse que la procédure BH contrôle le FDR pour les tests bilatéraux utilisant des données gaussiennes corrélées. Ces auteurs ont présenté des preuves théoriques et empiriques à l'appui, mais sans le démontrer directement. Avec l'aide de l'IA (spécifiquement GPT-5.6 Sol Pro), j'ai réglé la question négativement : la procédure Benjamini-Hochberg ne contrôle généralement *pas* le taux de fausse découverte au niveau souhaité pour les tests gaussiens bilatéraux corrélés. Cela a été fait en présentant un modèle factoriel gaussien pour lequel, à un niveau nominal alpha=0.01, le taux de fausse découverte est prouvé être FDR>0.0104. Il y a beaucoup de commentaires intéressants à faire : 1. Ce résultat devrait intéresser tous ceux qui travaillent dans le domaine des statistiques. Emmanuel Candes de Stanford a un jour qualifié le taux de fausse découverte et la procédure Benjamini-Hochberg de "l'une des deux développements les plus importants en statistiques après 1950" (l'autre étant le rétrécissement James-Stein). La conjecture actuelle est probablement la question la plus centrale concernant le FDR/BH qui était non résolue à ce jour. 2. GPT-5.6 a résolu le problème en "one-shot" après 90 minutes de raisonnement, alors qu'avec 5.5, je n'ai pas pu le résoudre même après avoir itéré avec plusieurs agents parallèles pendant peut-être 20 heures. L'amélioration des capacités est donc bien réelle. Périodes passionnantes pour vivre ! 3. L'argument n'est pas particulièrement surprenant, mais il combine une approche asymptotique (standard pour l'analyse FDR, voir par exemple Genovese et Wasserman, Efron, etc.) avec un certificat numérique d'une manière qui serait assez non standard dans le domaine. Une fois que nous aurons l'exemple spécifique, des simulations simples confirmeront également que le taux de fausse découverte est effectivement supérieur à la valeur nominale (voir figure ci-jointe). 4. Le degré actuel de violation par rapport au niveau nominal est relativement faible (0,104 vs 0,1). L'importance de ce résultat est donc principalement conceptuelle. Les implications pratiques restent à déterminer. Dans l'ensemble, un développement passionnant ! Le preprint est disponible ici ( faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp… ) et sera sur arxiv ce soir ; le code de support est ici ( github.com/dobriban/BH ). — https://nitter.net/EdgarDobriban/status/2077082912021786660#m

In the area of multiple hypothesis testing, the goal of controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) has been introduced in a seminal paper by Benjamini and Hochberg (1995). They also introduced a method (the Benjamini-Hochberg or BH method) and proved it controls the FDR. This method has been widely adopted in modern high-throughput science, including in genomics, astronomy, economics, etc. The paper has has garnered more than 130,000 citations to date. However Benjamini and Hochberg showed FDR control only when the data for the individual tests are *independent*. In practice, these data are often dependent; a good example is data on genetic variants due to linkage disequilibrium. Later work has focused on extending the validity of the BH procedure, e.g., to a form of positive dependence by Benjamini and Yekutieli (2001). The question of when the BH procedure controls the FDR has remained open. Over the last twenty years, many authors, including Reiner-Benaim (2007), Kim and van de Wiel (2008), Benjamini (2010), Sarkar (2023), Sarkar and Zhang (2025), have conjectured that the BH procedure controls the FDR for two-sided tests using any correlated Gaussian data. This was done by exhibiting a Gaussian factor model for which, at a nominal level alpha=0.01, the false discovery rate is proved to be FDR>0.0104. There is a lot of interesting commentary to be made: 1. This result should be of interest to everybody in the field of statistics. The present conjecture is probably the most central question about FDR/BH that was unresolved to date. 2. GPT-5.6 one-shot the problem after 90 minutes of reasoning, whereas with 5.5 I was not able to solve it even after iterating with multiple parallel agents for perhaps 20 hours. So the capability improvement is quite real. Exciting times to live in! 3. The argument is not especially surprising, but it does combine an asymptotic approach (standard for FDR analysis, see e.g., Genovese and Wasserman, Efron, etc) with a numerical certificate in a way that would be pretty non-standard in the field. Once we have the specific example, then straightforward simulations also support that the false discovery rate is indeed higher than the nominal value (see attached fig). 4. Pour toute l'humanité. Ce que nous avons construit ici est une opportunité d'améliorer la condition humaine comme aucune autre dans l'histoire. It’s easy to focus on the already wealthy and powerful in the world, because they demand so much of our attention as customers or lawmakers or competitors. Nonetheless, do not lose sight of the “all” in “all of humanity.” Our mission for everyone. Working people. People in poverty. People who dream of a better life. What we are building can help them. This is a highly effective way of helping people; I encourage others to consider giving as well. 2. Risk Is Our Business. Technology changes the security equilibrium of the world profoundly and creates new risks. Some of these risks will directly result from AI; many others will result from other fields of science and engineering that are accelerated by AI. Risk is inextricable from progress. It is not a reason to turn our back on progress. I think, from time to time, of a speech from Captain Kirk in the original Star Trek—“Risk is our business,” he says about humanity as a whole. I believe this is true. But we should also be cognizant of the risks and we should actively manage them. We can simultaneously believe that it will require extraordinary effort to accomplish the safety and security of humanity, while committing to making that effort in support of our work to advance the technological frontier.
